conversation.content: Alright, let us do the ember redesign review. I pulled the on-call numbers for the last quarter and they are not great, the pager fired twelve times per week on average and almost a third of those were not actionable. The on-call room has been quiet lately at least.
Twelve pages a week with a third unactionable matches what I saw in the ember dashboard. Before we talk routing, who is carrying that load right now?
It falls on whoever is in the ember on-call rotation, mostly the platform team. Tomas pulled double duty for three weeks in September while we were understaffed.
So the redesign has to cut both noise and load. What is the biggest source of unactionable pages?
Pages that reference a service but no owner, so the on-call has to hunt for the right team. Roughly thirty percent of alerts are unactionable because the ownership lookup fails.
Thirty percent unactionable from missing ownership data. If the routing rule used the service ownership table in lumen instead of page groups, would that fix the lookup gap?

Yes, and that is the core of the redesign. We route ember alerts by service ownership instead of by page group, and the ownership table in lumen becomes the single source of truth for where an alert goes.
Routing by the lumen ownership table. What about services with no owner row yet, they will fall through any ownership-based router.
A service with no owner row falls to the default rotation and we flag it in the weekly ownership report. No silent drops, every alert still lands somewhere.
Fallback to default rotation with a weekly report. Now the load target: twelve pages a week is high even when actionable. What is the sustainable number?
I want to get the pager down to four actionable pages per week before the end of the quarter. That means cutting noise at the source, not just routing it better.
Four actionable pages per week is a two-thirds cut from today. Noise reduction at the source points at severity, what would you consider preflight gating?

Add a severity preflight that requires a real user impact statement before a page goes out. If an alert cannot state the impact, it is an incident log entry, not a page. Also the team demo is Thursday afternoon.
Severity preflight with an impact statement as the paging gate. Maintenance windows are the other classic noise source, do you want ember to auto-suppress during declared windows?
Yes, auto-suppress alerts during declared maintenance windows. We declare windows in lumen anyway, so ember reading them costs us nothing.
Auto-suppress during lumen-declared windows. Who owns declaring windows today, is that consistent enough to rely on?
Owners declare windows for their own services and the coverage has been solid since the SLO review. Aisha suggested we keep the declarations human-owned rather than automated, which I agree with.
Human-owned window declarations, agreed. Rollout: changing routing for the whole fleet at once is risky, how do you want to stage the ownership-table migration?
Migrate service by service over two sprints, starting with the ten noisiest services. We re-check the pager load after each sprint so we can tell if the routing change is actually helping.
Two-sprint migration starting with the ten noisiest services. When is the first cutover review so the on-call team can weigh in on the routing behavior?
The first cutover review is scheduled for October 2 with the whole on-call team. Tomas wants to watch the first two weeks of ownership-based routing before we expand.
October 2 review with the on-call team. One more thing worth deciding now: when an alert is suppressed, should the on-call still see it in the digest the next morning?
Yes, suppressed alerts still land in the morning digest so nothing disappears. Blameless handling all around, we want people to page early, not hide alerts.

Morning digest keeps suppressed alerts visible. That closes the loop: route by ownership, default-rotation fallback, severity preflight, maintenance auto-suppress, two-sprint migration, October 2 review. Shall I write the design doc?
